title: JANUS Genesis — acetate source equivalence / context test
classification_note: Self-classified for registry navigation; not an independent biological or clinical validation.
purpose: Test whether acetate produced by an engineered SCOBY/acetic-acid-bacteria system should be modeled as intrinsically different from acetate arising after food fermentation, while separating molecular identity from route, matrix, microbiome contact, exposure and provenance.

esp32_twai_can.role: TWAI/CAN telemetry and provenance separation abstraction

claim_ceiling: Genetic modification of a producer does not by itself create a new molecular species of acetate.
Purified acetate is not claimed to have a special metabolic effect because of GMO provenance.
Equal molecular identity does not imply equal physiological outcome when route, concentration-time profile, counter-ion, pH, microbial contact, or accompanying matrix differ.
Unpurified kombucha-like fermentation broth is not equivalent to purified acetate.
The simulation does not establish safety, efficacy, nutrition, dosage, or clinical equivalence in humans.
No wet-lab genetic-engineering procedure or human dosing instruction is encoded.

experimental_design.principle: Source-blind metabolic comparison first; provenance is carried on a separate channel and must not affect the molecular-equivalence verdict.

frames.0x311: MATRIX_CONTEXT — route, pH, co-metabolite and microbial-context flags

can_profile.invariance_rule: The metabolic-equivalence verdict must ignore 0x312 provenance.

interpretation.primary_result: Within the source-blind model, matched purified acetate cannot be distinguished metabolically by producer provenance alone; differences arise when route, matrix, microbial contact, pH/counter-ion context, or an explicit analytical lineage marker differs.

colonic_acetate_systemic_availability_re.boundary: Stable-isotope study value recorded as evidence metadata, not a universal physiological constant.

evidence_constraints.colonic_cross_feeding: Reference stable-isotope work supports microbiota-dependent conversion/cross-feeding involving acetate; route therefore matters independently of molecular provenance.
evidence_constraints.kombucha_matrix: A kombucha-like fermentation matrix can contain multiple organic acids, residual ethanol, polyphenols, microbes and other metabolites; it must not be treated as acetate-only.

evidence_basis.claim_supported: Human tissues can take up and oxidize acetate.
Colonic acetate has route-dependent systemic availability and participates in microbiota cross-feeding.
Metabolic engineering of acetic-acid bacteria can alter acetic-acid production performance without implying a novel acetate molecular species.

next_gate: Replace binary matched/unmatched context flags with literature-bounded pharmacokinetic and fermentation-composition distributions, then test whether any residual source effect remains after chemistry, route, exposure and matrix are explicitly controlled.
